title: Understanding the Structure of QM7b and QM9 Quantum Mechanical Datasets Using Unsupervised Learning
summary: The paper asks how the internal structure of the QM7b and QM9 molecular datasets is organized and whether atomic composition can be predicted from quantum-derived properties for inverse molecular design. It applies intrinsic-dimension estimation, UMAP, tree-SNE/alpha-clustering, SUOD outlier detection, and regression-tree models predicting the number of atoms from original or 2D embedded features. The main result is that the intrinsic dimension is about 25% of the descriptor space, QM7b is two-cluster while QM9 has an inner clustered core plus an outlier shell, and atom count is highly predictable from original properties, with QM7b test MSE 0.1397 and R 0.9906.

match_target.why: Cheapest claim that still shows the paper's central predictability result: QM7b has only 7,211 molecules and 14 original properties, while QM9 has 133,885 molecules and is much more expensive; C1 is the paper's headline QM7b 14-original regression-tree row and matches the user hint.

tolerance.why: Rule 4: the primary target metric MSE is unbounded and the paper reports no std over repeated runs for this value, so use a 10% relative band around 0.1397; RMSE/MAE are treated analogously.

requirements.stmt: Use the QM7b dataset with 7,211 molecules and the 14 original property predictors.
requirements.quote: QM7b is composed of 7211 objects described in terms of 14 properties representing the inputs (Coulomb matrices).

requirements.stmt: Convert all original property values to z-scores before modeling.
Use zero-mean, unit-variance standardized properties as the common input scale.
requirements.quote: With the new variables having zero mean and unit variance, all properties are expressed in the same unit of measure

requirements.stmt: Set the prediction target to the number of atoms in the molecule.
requirements.cite: Section IV-A, regression tree predictability assessment
requirements.quote: using the number of atoms in the molecule as the target.

requirements.stmt: Evaluate regression tree models on a random 90%/10% training/testing split.
requirements.cite: Section IV-A, regression tree predictability assessment
requirements.quote: was made with regression tree models using a random 90%/10% training/testing split.

requirements.stmt: Use regression tree models rather than a complex black-box regressor.
requirements.cite: Section IV-A, regression tree predictability assessment
requirements.quote: They were used because of a trade-off between their simplicity and their ability to work with either a small or large number of predictor features

requirements.stmt: Report test-set MSE, RMSE, MAE, R, and nbrOfRules for QM7b and QM9 in Table II form.
requirements.quote: The results for the testing sets of both QM7b and QM9 are shown in Table II and Fig. 6.

requirements.stmt: For outlier analysis, use the SUOD ensemble with CBLOF, HBOS, LODA, LOF, and Isolation Forest.
requirements.quote: using the following combination of state-of-the-art individual techniques: CBLOF [17], HBOS [13], LODA [30], LOF [8], and Isolation Forest [24].

requirements.stmt: Compute tree-SNE dendrograms with 100 stacked alpha levels.
requirements.quote: The tree-SNE dendrogram was computed with 100 alpha levels in order to better appreciate the evolution of the successive embeddings in the hierarchy.

requirements.stmt: For the 2 generated features, use the canonical UMAP mapping composed with PCA to the target dimension.
requirements.quote: The final transformation is given by the function composition φ = (U ◦P)

requirements.stmt: Use t-SNE perplexity starting at 365 and decreasing to 1.06 for the tree-SNE hierarchy.
requirements.quote: a relatively higher value (365, because of the large size of the molecule dataset), to a small value (1.06)

requirements.stmt: Run 1,000 t-SNE iterations per level in the tree-SNE hierarchy.
requirements.quote: The number of iterations for the computation of the R19 →R t-SNE mappings required by each level was set to 1000 to ensure good convergence.
